look_here_first: Inspect mature leaf shape and tip: antelopehorns usually has much narrower lanceolate/linear-lanceolate leaves, narrowly tapering to an acute point. Check dense terminal flower heads, often more rounded than in A. viridis, but do not use head shape alone. Its five corona hoods are present; a projecting horn is not the reliable split from A. viridis.

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Herbaceous perennial from stout rootstocks; stems usually clustered, ascending to somewhat decumbent, about 20–60 cm tall.

key_traits.label: Leaf arrangement
key_traits.text: Alternate to subopposite, sometimes irregularly crowded; leaf arrangement overlaps with green milkweed.

key_traits.label: Leaf morphology
key_traits.text: Lanceolate to linear-lanceolate, about 1–3 cm wide, usually narrowly acuminate; often visibly narrower than A. viridis.

key_traits.label: Inflorescence
key_traits.text: Terminal, usually solitary, many-flowered and very crowded; peduncle length varies.

key_traits.label: Flower color
key_traits.text: Pale yellowish-green, sometimes purple-flushed; corona may show darker purple hoods.

key_traits.label: Gynostegium detail
key_traits.text: Five corona hoods are present. UT's detailed account of A. asperula subsp. capricornu describes each hood as lacking an enclosed horn. Do not teach 'A. asperula horned versus A. viridis hornless' as the species split; a hood is not the same thing as a horn. Subspecific hood color and form vary.

key_traits.label: Fruit
key_traits.text: Paired or solitary follicles; mature pods split to release comose seeds.

key_traits.label: Joey field note
key_traits.text: In Edwards Plateau Botany Part II, Joey shows a clear flowering umbel and uses the flower cluster to reinforce milkweed corona/hood structure.
